questions.question: Distinguish between breathing, gaseous exchange and cellular respiration, stating where each occurs and what kind of process it is.
questions.expected_answer: Breathing (ventilation) is the mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, in the chest. Gaseous exchange is the physical diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar and capillary walls in the lungs, and between blood and cells in the tissues. Cellular respiration is the chemical release of energy from glucose using oxygen in the mitochondria of every cell, producing carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: List four adaptations of the alveoli for gaseous exchange, giving the reason for each.
questions.expected_answer: About 300 million alveoli give a large surface area (about 70 m²) so that much gas can diffuse at once. Walls one cell thick give a short diffusion distance. A moist lining lets gases dissolve before crossing the membrane. A dense capillary network with constantly moving blood maintains a steep concentration gradient, as does breathing on the air side.

questions.question: Write the word and symbol equations for aerobic respiration and explain why a sprinter's muscles burn during a race and why breathing stays fast afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy; C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy, in the mitochondria. During a sprint oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough, so muscle cells respire partly anaerobically, breaking glucose down without oxygen to lactic acid with much less energy released; lactic acid accumulates and causes the burning and fatigue. Afterwards the lactic acid is carried to the liver and broken down using oxygen, so breathing and heart rate stay high until this oxygen debt is repaid.
